deep.reconstruction:
The page has three parts. None contains a mathematical derivation.

(A) Lines 1-3 finish the sentence from the previous page. That sentence belongs to the draft of the 12th Paris problem (1900): extending Kronecker's theorem that abelian fields over Q are cyclotomic. Hilbert proposes an analogue of Archimedes' repeated halving of the full angle and of Gauss's work. First, over a given ground field k, one should determine the extensions K/k whose relative degree is a power of 2 and whose relative discriminant has only prime factors dividing 2. He says these fields can be found and treated with the methods of inference used in his own papers. These are presumably the methods of his Zahlbericht and the 1898-99 work on relative quadratic and relative abelian fields and class fields.
The model case over Q (my illustration) is the tower Q(zeta_{2^n}). Its degree 2^(n-1) is a power of 2, and its discriminant is a power of 2. The real subfields Q(cos(2pi/2^n)) are generated by nested square roots, which is the algebraic form of Archimedean halving.

(B) The uniformization problem (later the 22nd problem). Problem: map an arbitrary continuum conformally onto the interior of the circle. Examples:
- a given Riemann surface (Poincare, Bull. Soc. Math. France 1883);
- a surface patch in space with arbitrary corners (Schwarz, Ges. Abh. pp. 167, 161-162, 72).
Hilbert restates this geometrically. Given are points, a set of directions through each point, and an angle between any two given directions; that is, a conformal structure. One should assemble 'straight lines' out of these points so that, using the given angles, one obtains a plane geometry. All of Hilbert's axioms (Grundlagen, 1899) should hold except the parallel axiom.
In modern terms: find a family of curves on the surface that serve as geodesics of a complete hyperbolic geometry whose angles agree with the given conformal angles. Equivalently, find a complete metric of curvature -1 conformal to the given structure.
On the disk this is exactly the Poincare model. Its lines are circular arcs orthogonal to the boundary, and its angles are the Euclidean ones. So the existence of such a geometry is equivalent to a conformal map onto the disk interior (the simply connected hyperbolic case).

(C) A methodological remark, a draft of rhetoric for the address:
- Number theory was once considered a field of lucky accidents and ideas.
- It no longer is, now that it has merged with algebra and interacts with geometry and function theory.
- Training in number theory is almost indispensable. Ignoring it is like learning a language while skipping its grammar.
- But one who does not use geometric intuition is like a blind man who must laboriously feel his way to the visible.
errors: No computational errors; there are no derivations.

Part (B) leaves conditions implicit. 'All axioms except the parallel axiom' (absolute geometry) does not by itself force hyperbolic geometry. Hilbert evidently means the hyperbolic plane, with angle congruence matching the given conformal angles. Without completeness and that matching condition, the reformulation is not equivalent to mapping onto the disk.
The reformulation also covers only the simply connected hyperbolic case. Parabolic cases (plane, sphere) and non-simply-connected surfaces (via the universal cover) are not addressed.
Line 2 is grammatically incomplete ('geht wenn man ...'). An adverb such as 'leicht' or 'glatt' seems to be missing.

results.what: Proposed first step toward the 12th problem: determine relative extensions of a given field with 2-power degree and relative discriminant divisible only by primes over 2, as an analogue of Archimedean angle halving and of Gauss.
results.modern_name: 2-ramified 2-extensions (pro-2 extensions unramified outside 2); Kronecker's Jugendtraum / Hilbert's 12th problem
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert, Paris problems 1900 (12th problem); class field theory by Takagi 1920; 2-ramified theory by Shafarevich, Koch and others later

results.what: Geometric reformulation of uniformization: from a conformal structure (points, directions, angles), construct lines giving a plane geometry satisfying all Hilbert axioms except the parallel axiom.
results.modern_name: Uniformization theorem via a conformal hyperbolic metric (Poincare disk model)
results.usually_credited_to: Uniformization by Koebe and Poincare (1907); the hyperbolic-metric viewpoint by Poincare and Klein

results.what: Remarks on number theory merging with algebra, geometry and function theory, and on its value for training mathematicians.
results.modern_name: Methodological remark (draft for the 1900 address and its themes)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (similar sentiments in the Zahlbericht preface 1897 and the 1900 address)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the 12th and 22nd problems of the 1900 address, both well known as Hilbert's. The new details are minor. One is the explicit 'halving' strategy via 2-power, 2-ramified extensions. The other is the axiomatic-geometric restatement of uniformization as building a non-Euclidean geometry from a conformal structure. That restatement links the Grundlagen to uniformization and is a nice unpublished detail, but it is not a new result.

checkable.asserts: Q(zeta_8) has degree 4, a power of 2, and its discriminant is a pure power of 2 (only the prime 2 ramifies).
Q(zeta_16) has degree 8 and discriminant 2^24; this is the 2-power, 2-ramified tower over Q.
Archimedean halving: cos(pi/8) is obtained by nested square roots, so the 16-gon is constructible.
The Poincare disk metric 4|dz|^2/(1-|z|^2)^2 has constant curvature -1. The disk interior thus carries a conformal geometry satisfying all axioms except the parallel axiom.
